1.—Department of Engineering Technology, Texas State University, San Marcos, TX, USA.
2.—Department of Materials Science and Engineering, Missouri University of Science and

Lightweight advanced high strength steels (AHSS) with aluminum contents
between 4 and 12 weight percent have been the subject of intense interest in
the last decade because of an excellent combination of high strain rate
toughness coupled with up to a 17% reduction in density. Fully austenitic cast
steels with a nominal composition of Fe-30%Mn-9%Al-0.9%C are almost 15%
less dense than quenched and tempered Cr-Mo steels (SAE 4130) with
equivalent strengths and dynamic fracture toughness. This article serves as a
review of the tensile and high-strain-rate fracture properties associated
mainly with silicon additions to this base composition. In the solution-treated
condition, cast steels have high work-hardening rates with elongations up to
64%, room-temperature Charpy V-notch (CVN) impact energies up to 200 J,
and dynamic fracture toughness over 700 kJ/m<sup>2</sup>. Silicon additions in the range
of 0.59–1.56% Si have no significant effect on the mechanical properties of
solution-treated steels but increased the tensile strength and hardness during
aging. For steels aged at 530-C to an average hardness of 310 Brinell hardness
number, HBW, increasing the amount of silicon from 1.07% to 1.56%
decreased the room temperature CVN breaking energy from 92 J to 68 J and
the dynamic fracture toughness from 376 kJ/m<sup>2</sup> to 265 kJ/m<sup>2</sup>. Notch tough-
ness is a strong function of phosphorus content, decreasing the solution-
treated CVN impact toughness from 200 J in a 0.006% P steel to 28 J in a
0.07% P steel. For age-hardened steels with 1% Si, increasing levels of phos-
phorus from 0.001% to 0.043% decreased the dynamic fracture toughness from
376 kJ/m<sup>2</sup> to 100 kJ/m<sup>2</sup>.

INTRODUCTION
High-manganese steels containing aluminum are
derived from Robert Hadfield’s original investigations
of a Fe-13wt.%Mn-1.2wt.%C steel with high tough-
ness and wear resistance.<sup>1</sup> All chemistry values are in
weight percent unless otherwise specified. Increasing
the manganese content to the range of 20–30% and
adding aluminum in levels up to 10% produces a fully
austenitic steel when solution treated above 950-C
and reduces the density of these steels up to 15% when
compared with conventional quench and tempered
steels. Therefore, these lightweight steels may be of
interest to the transportation industry as corporate
average fuel economy (CAFE) is ratcheted up to
54 mpg by 2025.<sup>2,3</sup> The lightweight steels with com-
positions in the range of 20–30% Mn, 5–11% Al, and
0.3–1.2% C obtain their strength as a result of age
hardening by the coherent precipitation of nanosized
j-carbide. These carbides precipitate homogeneously
in the austenitic matrix.<sup>2–6</sup> Mechanical properties are
a function of processing, composition, and age hard-
ening. Figure 1 compares representative microstruc-
tures of as-cast and hot-rolled and recrystallized fully
austenitic lightweight steels. As-cast alloys consist of
large primary austenitic dendrites that produce grain
structures on the order of millimeters. Hot rolling re-
fines the grain size, and the steel shown in Fig. 1b
consists of fine equiaxed austenite grains and
annealing twins. Hot- and cold-rolled solution-treated
steels have been shown to have exceptional strengths
and toughness with strengths as high as 2 GPa and
greater than 80% true fracture strain<sup>7,8</sup> In age-
hardened steels, strengths as high as 1210 MPa have
been reported by Acselrad et al.<sup>9</sup> for a wrought
Fe-29Mn-8.8Al-1C-1.33Si steel. Cast lightweight
steels have low melting points, less than 1350-C, and
excellent filling characteristics that are similar to cast
irons.<sup>2</sup> Recent studies of as-cast and age-hardened
Fe-30Mn-9Al-0.9C-(1–1.4)Si steels have shown that
these steels are competitive with quenched and tem-
pered Cr-Mo steels and can attain as high as
1085 MPa in tensile strength with greater than
400 kJ/m<sup>2</sup> of dynamic fracture toughness, depending
on the degree of age hardening.<sup>10,11</sup>

Recent research has focused on slight alloy
adjustments, mainly silicon, to nominal composition
Fe-30Mn-9Al-0.9C steels for use in the transporta-
tion industry, for military armor plate, as well as for
wear-resistant applications.<sup>3,10–16</sup>
However, the
high manganese content (20–30%) required to sta-
bilize a high aluminum austenitic matrix may rel-
egate these grades of steel to castings or casting
preforms that can be forged. Current steelmaking
practices for wrought product are limited to man-
ganese contents less than 8%, although Pohang Iron
and Steel Company (POSCO) has been successful
in producing second-generation advanced high-
strength steels that exhibit twin-induced plasticity
(TWIP) with 15–18% Mn. However, electrolytic
manganese is often required for these higher man-
ganese steels to limit temperature losses after
manganese addition, which drives the cost to that of
the Cr-Ni stainless steel grades.
Silicon is added to austenitic Fe-30Mn-9Al-0.9C
steel for a variety of different reasons. Silicon
additions increase the fluidity and decrease the
melting point by 30-C/wt.% Si, allowing for greater
flexibility of design and good filling of complex
shapes and thin sections.<sup>2</sup> Additionally, silicon has
been reported to prevent or suppress the formation
of brittle b-Mn during extended age hardening,<sub>17</sub>

High-strain-rate fracture in these lightweight steels
is also a function of phosphorus content and melt
cleanliness. Phosphorus in levels greater than 0.06% P
greatly increases the kinetics of age hardening but
sharply decreases the Charpy V-notch (CVN) impact
toughness by as much as 80%.<sup>13,16</sup> It is well known
that melting practice contributes to fracture because it
affects the composition, size, distribution, and mor-
phology of inclusions in steel. Schulte et al.<sup>19</sup> have
shown that the loss in CVN toughness in a Fe-30Mn-
9Al-1Si-0.9C steel is strongly correlated with
increasing amounts of AlN inclusions, which reduced
the CVN breaking energy at -40-C by almost 50%.

strain-rate fracture properties associated with cast
and wrought steels with a nominal composition of
Fe-30Mn-9Al-0.9C. The effect of silicon and phos-
phorus on strength and toughness during aging is
reviewed with respect to new and previously unpub-
lished findings. Table I gives the chemistry (wt.%) of
the respective steels discussed in this article.

The mechanism behind the hardening effect with
silicon addition has only recently been resolved by
Bartlett et al. for Fe-30Mn-9Al-(0.59–1.56)Si-0.9C-
0.5Mo cast steels.<sup>18</sup> This study used a combination
of transmission electron microscopy (TEM), 3-D
atom probe tomography (APT), x-ray diffraction
(XRD), and first principles modeling to study the
precipitation. In solution-treated specimens, XRD
and TEM results confirmed that, regardless of Si
content, no spinodal decomposition or short-range
ordering within the austenite had taken place.
However, increasing the amount of silicon acceler-
ated formation of j-carbide precipitates as shown in
Fig. 3 and appears to increase the volume fraction.
Silicon was shown by ab initio calculations and
experimental results to increase the activity of car-
bon in austenite and stabilize the j-carbide at
higher temperatures.<sup>18</sup> The repulsive Si-C interac-
tion was responsible for increasing the partitioning
coefficient of carbon in j-carbide from 2.1 to 2.9 in
0.59% and 1.56% Si steels aged 60 h at 530-C.<sup>18</sup>
Silicon was shown to partition to austenite during
aging and decrease the austenite lattice parameter.
Thus, as the silicon content of the austenite in-
creases, the repulsive interaction between silicon
and carbon forces an increase in carbon content of
the j-carbide to produce a corresponding increase in
the j-carbide lattice parameter. The respective
partitioning of carbon and silicon increases the c–j
constrained mismatch and increases the hardening
effect. The predicted increase in the yield
strength,<sup>18</sup> as determined using a spinodal hard-
ening mechanism derived from the work of Kato
et al.<sup>28</sup> was calculated to be 120 MPa/wt.% Si for
specimens aged at 530-C for 60 h, and this is in
reasonable agreement with previously reported
mechanical properties.

First-principles calculations have shown that sub-
stitution of phosphorus for aluminum positions in the
j-carbide is most favorable, and this is predicted to
create open-volume defects on {100} when a stress is
applied normal to the plane. Phosphorus substitution
for aluminum in the j-carbide structure as previously
reported by Medvedeva et al.<sup>29</sup> relaxes the local
bonding character along the h100ij. This results in a
45% reduction in the cleavage stress of the j-carbide
and is predicted to be the mechanism behind the
reduction in notch toughness of aged Fe-Mn-Al-C
steels containing phosphorus.<sup>29</sup> In more recent work,<sup>30</sup>
the effect of phosphorus on j-carbide precipitation in
Fe-30Mn-9Al-1Si-0.9C-0.5Mo cast steels was investi-
gated using a combination of TEM, three-dimensional
APT, and XRD. Phosphorus was shown to increase the
prevalence of the ordering reaction and high phos-
phorus, 0.043% P, specimens exhibited SRO that took
place during the quench and prior to spinodal decom-
position of the austenite. First-principles calculations
show that SRO of Fe-Al-C into the E2<sub>1</sub> crystal struc-
ture is energetically favorable over a homogeneous
solid solution.<sup>31</sup> In contrast, neither SRO nor spinodal
decomposition took place during the quench in the
previous study using low-phosphorus specimens.<sup>18</sup>
Phosphorus greatly increased the size and volume
fraction of j-carbide precipitation and accelerated both
the first-stage ordering reaction as well as concurrent
spinodal decomposition. Figure 4 shows the dark-field
TEM h100i<sub>j</sub> images of a 0.001% P and 0.043% P Fe-
30Mn-9Al-1Si-0.9C-0.5Mo steel aged for 0.5 h at
570-C. In the low-phosphorus steel, there is a high
number density of small (a few unit cells in dimension)
ordered domains that exhibit diffraction intensity
corresponding to the perovskite crystal structure of j-
carbide (see Fig. 4a). In the high-phosphorus steel,
these ordered domains are much larger at an average
size of 5 nm and are preferentially coarsening along
h100ic as shown in Fig. 4b. One of the most important
results from this study is that phosphorus was found
to be randomly distributed between the matrix and the
j-carbide, and the increase in the rate of hardening
with increasing phosphorus content is therefore not
related to long-range diffusion of phosphorus. Instead,
it was found that phosphorus greatly increases the
rate of spinodal decomposition during aging at 530-C
as shown in Fig. 5.
Increasing levels of P from 0.006% to 0.043% P
increased the diffusion of carbon during aging, and
after 10 h at 530-C, the carbon amplitude varied
from 4.4 at.% to 6.0 at.%, respectively. It is there-
fore suggested that phosphorus increases the initial
ordering reaction and that this greatly accelerates
the later stage of spinodal decomposition. First-
principles calculations show that phosphorus sub-
stitutions for aluminum corner positions in j-car-
bide are most energetically favorable, and this may
be responsible for the enhancement of the ordering
reaction in the high-phosphorus alloys.<sup>29</sup>
A random walk estimate of the SRO kinetics of
phosphorus atoms and aluminum atoms into j-car-
bide corner positions during quenching was calcu-

for high energy-absorbing applications, knowledge
of the high-strain-rate fracture toughness, or
dynamic fracture toughness, in the presence of a
sharp crack is desired. For ductile materials exhib-
